one_liner: A command-line tool that takes a sample of an AI app's logged prompts, replays them against two models with your own API keys, and prints the cost gap for each call site next to a diff of the outputs.
who: A solo developer running a free or cheap public AI app on pay-per-token APIs who keeps the logs of last week's generations.
moment: They have hand-built cost controls (per-user and per-IP hourly limits, daily circuit breakers, hard spend caps) and only discover by accident, after a week in production, that one model cost about ten times another for the same work.
why_now: From the evidence: new models keep arriving at listed prices well below their predecessors (gpt-6.1-sol at $2/$10 per 1M tokens, half of gpt-5.6-sol), and one developer saw a 10x gap between two cheap models over 7 days. Choosing a model is now a recurring decision, and a week of production is an expensive way to make it.

existing.name: promptfoo
existing.does: Runs a set of prompts or test cases against several providers side by side and reports outputs, latency and cost.
existing.lacks: It is built around hand-written eval suites rather than ingesting an app's own generation logs, and it does not group the cost gap by the app's call sites.

existing.name: Langfuse / Helicone (LLM observability)
existing.does: Log production generations with token counts and cost, and offer datasets or experiments to rerun prompts.
existing.lacks: They need the app routed through their SDK or proxy before the week being analysed, and they are hosted or heavy services rather than a one-shot replay over logs the developer already has.

existing.name: LiteLLM / OpenRouter
existing.does: Provide one API across many models with per-request cost tracking.
existing.lacks: They track cost for live traffic and do not replay past logs against a second model or compare outputs.

score_reasons.buildability: The tool is a small loop of log reading, two API calls per prompt, a price table and a report. The hard parts are the variety of log formats and needing the user's own provider keys to test it end to end.
score_reasons.insight: Replaying logs as shadow traffic to choose a model is a fair transfer from web infrastructure, but anyone who has seen a price sheet would think of it. The 10x gap is a good hook, not a hidden connection.
score_reasons.differentiation: promptfoo already compares prompts across models with cost, and observability tools already log cost. The only real difference is ingesting existing logs and breaking down by call site, which is a thin wedge.
score_reasons.grounding: The person, the 10x gap and the cost-control pain trace to E1, and the price churn traces to E2. Per-call-site breakdown, output diffing and the 100-prompt replay are the idea's own mechanism and do not appear in the evidence.

buildability_reasons: Core scope is small: read a log file, sample prompts, call two models, multiply reported tokens by a price table, and print a table plus diffs.
Logs come in many shapes (JSONL, CSV, provider exports), so v1 must pick a simple input contract and a field mapping.
It needs the user's own API keys for two providers. That is fine for users but awkward for the builder to verify without a stub provider.
Prices change often, so a user-editable price table is needed instead of hard-coded rates.
risks: Output equivalence is a judgement. The tool can show diffs but cannot say whether the cheaper model is good enough.
Gateways and observability tools (promptfoo, Langfuse, OpenRouter) may add log replay and make this redundant.
Small apps may not keep logs, or keep them without the full prompt and call-site tag.
Demand rests on a single developer's post. The signal score is very low and only one citation survived checking.
Replaying prompts that contain user data through a second provider may conflict with the app's privacy promises.
brief: A developer running a free AI app on pay-per-token APIs hand-built rate limits and spend caps, and only found out by accident after a week that one model cost about ten times another for the same generations. Build something they can point at last week's logged prompts that replays a sample against two models with their own keys, then prints the cost gap per call site alongside a diff of the outputs, so they can judge whether the cheaper model is good enough before switching instead of after a week of production.
grounding: A developer reports $3.81 for 478 generations on Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite versus $0.39 for 467 generations on GPT-6 Luna over 7 days.

The developer runs a free AI app (DX7 AI Studio, which uses LLMs to edit synthesizer patches) and describes per-user and per-IP hourly limits, daily circuit breakers, and hard spend caps at the API provider level.
A Mastodon post lists a price of $2/$10 per 1M tokens for gpt-6.1-sol, half the price of gpt-5.6-sol.
Thesis: The data to choose a model is already in the app's logs; replaying it is cheaper than a week of production.
Smallest useful v1: A script that replays 100 logged prompts against two models and prints the per-call-site cost and an output diff.
Cheapest test: Replay 100 prompts from one app; it is real if the report finds a gap of at least 2x on one call site with outputs the developer judges equivalent.
Risks: Output equivalence is a judgement; gateways may add this; apps may not keep logs.
cheapest_test: Replay 100 prompts from one real app's logs against two models. The idea is real if the report finds a gap of at least 2x on one call site with outputs the developer judges equivalent.

claims.claim: Replay a week of a small AI app's prompts
claims.interpreted: Replay a sample drawn from the logs the developer supplies (by default the most recent week), capped at a set number of prompts so cost stays bounded.

setting.means: Maximum number of logged prompts replayed per run

claims.why: A capped sample of last week's traffic still shows the cost gap, which is the point, without paying to rerun every call.

claims.claim: print the cost gap per call site
claims.interpreted: Cost is computed from the token usage each provider reports, multiplied by a user-editable price table. Prompts are grouped by a call-site field the user names in the logs, or treated as one site when no such field exists.

setting.means: Log field used to group prompts into call sites

claims.why: Grouping by whatever tag the app already logs still shows where the money goes. Using reported tokens keeps the numbers honest as prices change.

claims.claim: an output diff (outputs the developer judges equivalent)
claims.interpreted: The tool shows the two models' outputs side by side with a diff for the developer to judge. It does not decide equivalence itself.
claims.why: The idea already says equivalence is the developer's judgement. Putting the evidence in front of them is the useful part.
